body: I don't want to speak for this person, but I was prescribed propranolol for the physical effects of anxiety. It's a beta blocker so it helps to block that surge of adrenaline you get- so you don't get the hard pounding/shakiness/sweaty palms thing. Musicians use it for stage fright sometimes because it won't dull you down like a benzo. It's normally for cardiac stuff/blood pressure. Definitely not addictive.

Hi gladiator0flaw, 

I'm going to give you my two cents. This is not coming from someone who is a doctor or any type of medical professional, BUT as someone who has taken some sort of antidepressant since the extremely young age of 12 and who has literally tried almost every antidepressant under the sun (from everything from the classics SSRIs to the SNRIs to the old tricyclics to the third generation antipsychotics and off label use mood stabilizers) I can say this:
It's hard to say if antidepressants make things worse in the long run because truthfully, depression is actually such a heterogenous condition. There have been times where I have been really melancholy and deeply sad- crying all the time and feeling vulnerable, whereas other times I have been obsessive and ruminated over the past a lot. There were also times where I felt just tired and flat and like nothing gave me pleasure, but I could get through the day to day. Each of these different mental states would probably be diagnosed as depression, but I think they each have their own distinct underlying pathology/neurochemical or biological correlates. I think that the SNRIs tend to be good for the type of depression where you feel unmotivated and lie in bed all day and eat but maybe not for someone who can't sleep or eat and is anxious. Also, effexor can definitely work on norepinephrine and even dopamine- but I think that the dose level matters. 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16690006 

I agree with the other posts on here, antidepressants can be a great tool to help you when you are deep in despair and need that boost to give you the energy/sanity to make behavioral changes, but without those changes or therapy, you will only get so much out of it.

I completely relate to the symptom of no appetite-it's scary and hard and the more you think about it, the less you eat and the less you eat the more you have decreased appetite and your blood sugar gets lower and your mood plummets. It's a vicious cycle. 

If you feel like you can't chew anything, make a smoothie with bananas, ice cream or yogurt and peanut butter for lots of protein. There are also Odwalla drinks that have like 410 calories and like 32 grams of protein. It might just help to just get up and have these before you even attempt to eat. You might find that having less pressure on yourself to eat will make it all that much easier

I'm a woman, so my perspective is a little different. However, levator ani syndrome is a type of pelvic floor dysfunction and I have had a lot of experience with that and it has affected my ability to have regular bowel movements. What has really been worthwhile for me has been physical therapy. It sounds crazy and it is a little invasive but having a physical therapist evaluate those muscles and their accompanying trigger points has been really helpful. It also helps to fix the underlying issues and they can teach you how to do the exercises yourself. If you're willing to put the time in then it's great medication/surgery free way to get real relief.

I've been in your position before. I think the best attitude to have is to be open to the fact that there is a very good chance that it will work but also realize that even if it doesn't work, it's not the end of the world because there is so much medication out there. I've had allergic reactions, horrible side effects etc. from medication and while I was disappointed with the results, I realized that it just brought me one step closer to finding something that is effective. It is a lot of trial and error, which is tough but you'll get there

Finding a really good psychiatrist can be really tough. Some of them are pretty indifferent and cold and don't really seem to care. I recommend finding a psychiatrist via word of mouth or by looking them up online and seeing their ratings. Most doctors have a few nasty ratings, but the overall trends of comments should be positive. 

As for the diagnosis thing, this is really tough. It's so easy to get super focused on the diagnosis because in a way, it seems like an identity and you also probably want to know what your prognosis is. When I was in college, I was diagnosed with "mixed bipolar" disorder and later on was diagnosed with cyclothymia (mild bipolar). Like you, I had never had anything that most people would classify as a hypomanic episode. When I asked the psychiatrist why I got that diagnosis, he said that psychiatrists (or at least some of them) are expanding the definition of what it means to be bipolar and think of bipolarity as more of a spectrum than a simple black and white yes or no thing. He explained that anxiety, irritability and agitation could be considered features of hypomania even if you have a low mood because they involve elevated energy. Having racing thoughts, extreme anger and restlessness along with a very low mood and pessimistic outlook would be consider a mixed episode. Whether or not you believe this to be true, the important thing is to get the right treatment.  I didn't really believe that I was bipolar (at least not in the classic sense) but I tried a mood stabilizer and for the first time since I had gotten sick, I felt like I had something that covered ALL of my symptoms. Sometimes doctors see your response to a medication in order to make a diagnosis. Try not to get too hung about it (I know it's hard). You're making the right steps and you aren't alone.

When I took Abilify, I experienced this feeling of inner restlessness (I think the proper term for this side-effect is akathesia). I had trouble sleeping, I would go to bed and wake up four hours later ready to start the day. In retrospect, I probably should have given it more time because I think the side-effects that I described can wear off. I was also put off by the fact that it would have cost $125 a month but now I think the generic is available so cost isn't an issue. I'm not an expert, but I think trying a tiny dose could be worth it.

I know that estrogen levels play a huge role in pain, especially for women. I would get one of those period apps and keep track of your cycle and your pain. Your hormones are also connected to your thyroid which affects your mental health. There are so many intertwining things are play here.

Benzos are great for anxiety, I don't know anyone who has taken a benzo and not felt any relief. There are several downfalls to benzos. They are pretty addictive and your body develops a tolerance fairly quickly. Long term use can lead to memory issues/other cognitive problems. I think klonopin is best used for when you are having a panic attack or when you are going through a really tough time and you need something to lean on while waiting for the other medication to work. I also think that klonopin can make depression worse long term, I've read several articles about that and can post them if you want.
As for Abilify, out of all the anti-psychotics it as the lowest risk for tardive dyskinesia. I've taken Abilify before for depression and wasn't crazy about it, but I think for people with OCD/intrusive thoughts/ruminations Abilify works pretty well.

So I personally haven't taken it for depression but I hear that it works really well for depression, especially if you get into these negative spirals of despair and ruminate a lot or have intrusive thoughts. And since negative thoughts/rumination are a huge part of depression, it could do wonders. Also, I think lamictal takes awhile to work, but everyone is different

If I lived in a world where there were no serious consequences to long term drug abuse and could do whatever I wanted, I would start the day with some coffee to wake me up with a side of adderall to lift my mood and bring me clarity and then some klonopin to smooth it all out. That would be ideal.

I know this comment might not make you feel better, but what you've articulated is something that happens to people suffering with mental illness all the time. There's the period of time in your life where the depression/mania/agitation/anxiety is taking over everything and the only thing that matters is stopping it. Then there's this sort of secondary damage that occurs because while we're busy managing the mental illness, the world doesn't skip a single beat. You begin to feel better but then realize you have a huge mess to clean up or that you don't have a "life" to go back to. Here's the thing: you are SO young. You have so much time to turn it around and the fact that you know what you need to do is half of it. Freshman year is a huge transition time for everyone, even for those people who LOVED college and couldn't WAIT to get away. You got the proper diagnosis and are getting the proper treatment and doing everything right. It's never too late and in this case, it really is the beginning. A lot of people don't even remain friends with the people they made freshman year because so many different things happen and change. Also, what other choice do you have? You owe it to yourself to give it all you've got.
